stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. uses Microsoft Entra Agent ID and has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses. Many agent identities were created for pilot projects that ended months ago. You plan an Agent ID lifecycle policy.

You need the policy to flag agent identities for which no tokens were issued during the last 90 days.

Which lifecycle rule should you enable?
choices: Inactivity monitoring
Periodic reconfirmation
Minimum sponsor requirement
Fallback recipient notification
explanation: An Agent ID lifecycle policy has three rules: periodic reconfirmation (is the agent still needed), minimum sponsor requirement (is someone accountable) and inactivity monitoring (has the identity been used). Inactivity is measured by token issuance, so it is the rule for stale identities.
rationale: Correct: inactivity monitoring treats an agent identity as inactive when no tokens were issued for it during the configured duration, which is exactly the 90-day unused signal the stem asks for.

Incorrect: periodic reconfirmation asks the sponsor or owner to confirm every 30 to 730 days that the agent is still required, whether or not it is used. Use it when the business must re-attest need on a schedule.

Incorrect: the minimum sponsor requirement flags agent identities that have fewer sponsors than the configured number. Use it to prevent orphaned agents, not to detect agents that stopped requesting tokens.

Incorrect: fallback recipients are a notification setting of the policy, not a rule. They receive notices when an agent identity has no sponsor or owner. Add them in addition to a rule, never instead of one.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses and Microsoft Entra ID P1. You are an AI Administrator.

You need to create an Agent ID lifecycle policy that disables agent identities that their sponsors no longer confirm.

Which location should you use to create the policy?
choices: Entra admin center > ID Governance > Lifecycle Workflows > Lifecycle Policies
Entra admin center > Entra ID > Agents > Agent identities
Entra admin center > ID Governance > Entitlement management
Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > Settings > Agent management rules
explanation: Agent ID lifecycle policies live under Lifecycle Workflows in ID Governance of the Microsoft Entra admin center (Lifecycle Policies > Agent ID (Preview)). The Lifecycle Workflows Administrator and AI Administrator roles can create them. The policy evaluates rules, notifies sponsors and then disables or deletes the identity.
rationale: Correct: Agent ID lifecycle policies are created under ID Governance > Lifecycle Workflows > Lifecycle Policies > Agent ID (Preview), and the AI Administrator role is one of the two roles that can create them.

Incorrect: the Agent identities page lets an administrator view agents and disable selected ones manually, including several at once. Use it for an immediate one-off action, not for an automatic rule based on sponsor confirmation.

Incorrect: entitlement management access packages grant time-bound group memberships, roles and API permissions to agent identities. Their expiration removes access, not the identity. Use them to govern what an agent can reach.

Incorrect: agent management rules run bulk actions on registry entries, such as blocking ownerless agents. They do not evaluate sponsor reconfirmation of Entra agent identities. Use them for registry governance at scale.

stem:
Litware, Inc. has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses. Employees sponsor many agent identities. HR sets the employeeLeaveDateTime attribute for each employee who leaves.

On the last day of a departing sponsor, the sponsorships of that user must move to the user's manager automatically, and cosponsors must be notified.

What should you create?
choices: A workflow from the Transition agent sponsorships when a sponsor leaves template
A workflow from the Transition agent sponsorships when a sponsor changes roles template
An Agent ID lifecycle policy that has the minimum sponsor requirement rule enabled
A workflow from the Onboard new hire employee template with the sponsor tasks added
explanation: Two Lifecycle Workflows templates handle agent sponsorship: a leaver template (time based on employeeLeaveDateTime by default) and a mover template (attribute or group membership changes). Both contain the tasks to notify the manager, notify cosponsors and transfer sponsorships to the manager. Sponsor tasks exist only in mover and leaver workflows.
rationale: Correct: the leaver template triggers on employeeLeaveDateTime by default and includes Send email to co-sponsors about sponsor changes and Transfer agent sponsorships to manager, so both requirements are met on the last day.

Incorrect: the mover template triggers on attribute or group membership changes when a sponsor changes roles. The users in the stem leave the company, so the leave date trigger of the leaver template fits instead.

Incorrect: the minimum sponsor requirement only detects agent identities with too few sponsors and notifies or acts on them. It does not transfer sponsorship to a manager. Use it as a safety net for orphaned agents.
Incorrect: the sponsor tasks are mover and leaver tasks and cannot be added to a joiner template such as Onboard new hire employee. Use joiner templates for tasks that run when a user starts.

stem:
Tailspin Toys configures an Agent ID lifecycle policy that has periodic reconfirmation enabled.

When a sponsor does not reconfirm an agent identity in time, the identity must stop working immediately. If nobody acts during the following 30 days, the identity must then be deleted.

Which policy action should you select?
choices: Disable and delete, with a 30-day delete delay
Disable, with a grace period of 30 days
Delete, with a grace period of 30 days
Disable, with a fallback recipient added
explanation: Policy actions are Disable, Delete (soft delete) and Disable and delete. Disable and delete disables at once and deletes after a configurable number of days. A separate grace period delays the action itself to give sponsors time to remediate.
rationale: Correct: Disable and delete disables the agent identity immediately and deletes it after the number of days that you specify, which matches stop now and delete after 30 days.
Incorrect: Disable stops sign-ins but never deletes the identity, and a grace period only delays the disable itself. Use it when stale identities must stay recoverable indefinitely.

Incorrect: Delete soft deletes the identity, and the grace period postpones that action, so the agent keeps working during the 30 days. Use it when there is no need for an intermediate disabled state.
Incorrect: a fallback recipient only receives notifications when an agent has no sponsor or owner. It adds no deletion step. Add it when unaccountable agents must still reach a human.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank has an Agent ID lifecycle policy named Policy1 that covers all agent identities. You need to test a stricter policy on three test agent identities. Sponsors must reconfirm the agents every 30 days, unconfirmed agents must be disabled after a short grace period, and the new policy must win over Policy1 for the test agents.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: In the Microsoft Entra admin center, browse to ID Governance > Lifecycle Workflows > Lifecycle Policies > Agent ID (Preview), and select New policy.
Enter a name, enable the policy, and select Specific agents as the scope with the three test agent identities.
Enable Periodic reconfirmation and set the frequency to 30 days.
Select the Disable policy action, enable the grace period, and then select Save.
In the policy list, move the new policy above Policy1.
Create a workflow from the Transition agent sponsorships when a sponsor leaves template.
Create an access package for the test agents that expires after 30 days.
explanation: A lifecycle policy is built in wizard order: create, scope, rules, action, save. Priority only exists for saved policies, and the highest-priority matching policy applies when an agent is in more than one policy. Testing with Specific agents and the minimum 30-day frequency is the pattern that Learn recommends.
rationale: Step 1: Agent ID lifecycle policies are created from the Agent ID (Preview) page under Lifecycle Policies, so you start there with New policy.
Step 2: the basics of the policy come first, and Specific agents limits it to the three test identities so that the test does not affect production agents.
Step 3: periodic reconfirmation is the rule that asks sponsors to confirm need; 30 days is the minimum allowed frequency and the one Learn suggests for tests.
Step 4: the action defines what happens to unconfirmed agents; Disable with a grace period gives sponsors a short window, and saving creates the policy.
Step 5: priority can only be set on existing policies. Moving the new policy above Policy1 makes it the highest-priority match for the overlapping test agents.
Incorrect: this leaver workflow transfers sponsorships when a sponsor leaves the company. It does not ask for reconfirmation or disable agents. Use it to keep sponsorship current when people leave.
Incorrect: an expiring access package removes the access it granted, but the agent identity stays enabled and nobody is asked to reconfirm. Use access packages for time-bound resource access.

stem:
Relecloud has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses and Microsoft Entra ID P1. You are creating an Agent ID lifecycle policy with these requirements:

- Sponsors must confirm every 180 days that each agent identity is still needed.
- An agent identity that is not confirmed must be blocked from sign-in but must never be deleted by the policy.
- Sponsors must be able to confirm agents without an admin role.

How should you configure the policy? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
explanation: Pick the rule by the question it answers (still needed, still accountable, still used), the action by how reversible it must be, and remember that sponsors act in the Manage agents experience of the My Account portal.

targets.label: Lifecycle rule
why: Correct: periodic reconfirmation asks the sponsor or owner to confirm at a set frequency (30 to 730 days) that the agent is still required, so 180 days fits.
Incorrect: inactivity monitoring reacts to agents that received no tokens for a period, so an agent in daily use would never be reviewed. Use it to catch stale identities.
Incorrect: the minimum sponsor requirement checks how many sponsors an agent has and never asks anyone to confirm need. Use it to prevent orphaned agents.

targets.label: Policy action
why: Correct: Disable prevents future sign-ins and usage but keeps the identity, which meets blocked but never deleted.
Incorrect: Delete soft deletes the agent identity, which the requirement forbids. Use it when unconfirmed agents should be removed directly.
Incorrect: Disable and delete removes the identity after a set number of days. Use it when disabled agents must be cleaned up later.

targets.label: Where sponsors confirm
options: Manage agents in the My Account portal
Access packages in the My Access portal
Requests tab in the Microsoft 365 admin center
why: Correct: sponsors and owners reconfirm (Extend) or disable agent identities in the Manage agents experience at myaccount.microsoft.com/agents, without an admin role.
Incorrect: in My Access, sponsors request access packages on behalf of agents; reconfirmation is not done there. Use it when an agent needs more access.
Incorrect: the Requests tab is where AI Administrators review publish and activation requests. Sponsors without an admin role cannot use it.

stem:
Refer to the case study. You need to meet the agent identity lifecycle requirements.

What should you configure?
choices: An Agent ID lifecycle policy with 60-day inactivity monitoring, the Disable action, and User5 as fallback recipient
A workflow from the Transition agent sponsorships when a sponsor leaves template, scoped to all sponsors
An access review of all agent identities that uses sponsors as reviewers and auto-applies deny results
An agent management rule that blocks ownerless agents without usage, run by User5 every 60 days
explanation: Agent ID lifecycle policies combine a rule (here inactivity, measured by token issuance), an action (Disable keeps the identity recoverable) and notifications that go to sponsors, owners or fallback recipients. Fallback recipients cover agents that have no accountable person.
rationale: Correct: inactivity monitoring catches agent identities without token issuance for 60 days, Disable blocks them without deletion, sponsors are notified, and User5 as fallback recipient covers agents that have no sponsor.
Incorrect: this leaver workflow moves sponsorships to a manager when a sponsor leaves. It never looks at agent usage and never disables an agent. Use it to keep sponsorship current.

Incorrect: an access review removes access assignments, such as group memberships, based on reviewer decisions. It does not detect token inactivity or disable the identity. Use it for periodic attestation of access.

Incorrect: this agent management rule in the Microsoft 365 admin center blocks registry entries of ownerless agents that have no usage. It does not evaluate token issuance of Entra agent identities, ignores inactive agents that still have a sponsor, and does not disable the identity. Use it to contain abandoned ownerless agents in the registry.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. is building a leaver workflow in Lifecycle Workflows for employees who sponsor agent identities.

The workflow must add each departing user's manager as a sponsor of the agent identities and remove the departing user as a sponsor.

Which task should you add to the workflow?
choices: Transfer agent identity sponsorships to manager
Send email to manager about sponsorship changes
Send email to co-sponsors about sponsor changes
Revoke all refresh tokens for user
explanation: Lifecycle Workflows has three sponsor tasks: two notification tasks and one transfer task. Only the transfer task changes the sponsor relationship, and it needs a populated manager attribute on the departing user.
rationale: Correct: this task finds every agent identity the user sponsors, adds the user's manager as a sponsor and removes the user, which is exactly the required change.
Incorrect: this task only emails the manager that the user sponsored agent identities, so the manager can choose a new sponsor. It changes nothing by itself. Use it when a human must decide.
Incorrect: this task informs the other sponsors of each agent about the change. It does not add or remove sponsors. Use it so cosponsors know they are now accountable.
Incorrect: this leaver task revokes the user's refresh tokens to end the user's sessions. It does not touch sponsorships. Use it to cut off access of a departing user.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. has a fleet of customer support agents that use Microsoft Entra Agent ID agent identities. You create an access package that grants membership in a security group. The agents must be able to request the access package programmatically.

In the access package policy, you select For users, service principals, and agent identities in your directory.

Which scope should you select?
choices: All agents
All service principals
All members (excluding guests)
Specific users and groups
explanation: An access package policy decides who can request it. For agents that use Entra agent identities, choose For users, service principals, and agent identities in your directory and then All agents. Agents that still use plain service principals need a separate policy with All service principals.
rationale: Correct: All agents lets every agent identity in the directory request the package, which is what the support agents with Entra agent identities need to submit their own assignment requests.

Incorrect: All service principals covers agents that authenticate with classic service principals instead of agent identities. Add a second policy with this scope only when some agents are not on Agent ID.
Incorrect: All members (excluding guests) lets human member users request the package. Agent identities are not users, so the agents could not request it. Use it for employee access packages.
Incorrect: Specific users and groups limits requests to selected users or group members. Agent identities are not added this way. Use it to restrict a package to one team of people.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. has an agent named Agent1 that uses a Microsoft Entra agent identity. Agent1 must read documents in a SharePoint Online site named Site1. Members of a security group named Group1 have read permission on Site1.

You create a new access package for Agent1.

Which resource role should you add to the access package?
choices: Member of Group1
Read role on the Site1 SharePoint Online site
An application role of the SharePoint app
A role in the SAP cloud application
explanation: Access packages for agent identities can contain security group memberships, Microsoft Entra roles and OAuth API permissions. They cannot contain application roles, SAP roles or SharePoint Online site roles. Use a group that already has the site permission to reach SharePoint content.
rationale: Correct: security group membership is a supported resource role for agent identities, and Group1 already has read permission on Site1, so membership gives Agent1 the access it needs.
Incorrect: SharePoint Online site roles cannot be assigned to agent identities through access packages. Use a site role in access packages for human users only.
Incorrect: application roles cannot be assigned to agent identities or service principals through access packages. Use them in packages for users who sign in to an enterprise application.
Incorrect: SAP roles are also excluded for agent identities, and SAP is unrelated to SharePoint access. Use SAP roles in access packages that govern SAP access for users.

stem:
Relecloud must create an access package for agent identities that contains only membership in two security groups. Agents will request it, and a manager will approve each request.

You need to create the access package by using the least privileged role.

Which role should you use?
choices: Identity Governance Administrator
Global Administrator
Conditional Access Administrator
Lifecycle Workflows Administrator
explanation: Creating access packages requires at least Identity Governance Administrator. Only when OAuth API permissions or directory roles are added as resource roles does Learn require Global Administrator, and the catalog becomes privileged.
rationale: Correct: Identity Governance Administrator can create catalogs and access packages with group resource roles, which is all this package contains, so it is the narrowest role that works.
Incorrect: Global Administrator is required only when the package includes OAuth API permissions or directory roles. For group memberships it is broader than needed.
Incorrect: Conditional Access Administrator manages Conditional Access policies, including policies for agents, but not entitlement management. Use it to block or allow agent token issuance.
Incorrect: Lifecycle Workflows Administrator manages workflows and Agent ID lifecycle policies, not access packages. Use it for sponsor transfer and inactivity automation.

stem:
Northwind Traders has an agent named Agent1. Agent1 reads the mailbox of the signed-in user when the user chats with it. At night, Agent1 also processes orders by using its own agent's user account. Agent1 calls a partner service that authenticates by using an API key.

You create a Conditional Access policy that is assigned to Agents and includes the agent identity of Agent1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: The policy applies when Agent1 signs in with its agent's user account.
When Agent1 reads mail for a signed-in user, the policies assigned to that user are evaluated.
The policy applies when Agent1 calls the partner service with the API key.
explanation: Conditional Access evaluates the token subject: the user in on-behalf-of access, the agent identity in app-only access and the agent's user account in agent-user access. Each subject needs its own policy, and resources that do not use Microsoft Entra tokens are outside Conditional Access.
rationale: No: a policy that targets an agent identity does not apply to the agent's user account. To cover the night processing, create a separate policy that targets agent users.
Yes: in the on-behalf-of flow the signed-in user is the token subject, so Conditional Access evaluates policies assigned to that user, not the policy that targets the agent identity.

No: Conditional Access only protects token issuance by Microsoft Entra ID. A call that uses an API key bypasses that pipeline, so no policy applies. Move the service to Entra authentication to control it.

stem:
Tailspin Toys has an access package named Agent Mail Access. Its first assignment policy allows All agents to get access. You need to directly assign the agent identity of Agent1 to the access package by using Microsoft Graph PowerShell.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "EntitlementManagement.ReadWrite.All"`
`$ap = Get-MgEntitlementManagementAccessPackage -Filter "displayName eq 'Agent Mail Access'" -ExpandProperty "assignmentPolicies"`
Build `$params` with `requestType = "adminAdd"`, the object ID of Agent1 as `targetId`, `$ap.AssignmentPolicies[0].Id` and `$ap.Id`.
`New-MgEntitlementManagementAssignmentRequest -BodyParameter $params`
`New-MgEntitlementManagementAssignmentPolicy -BodyParameter $params`
`Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Application.ReadWrite.All"`
`New-MgEntitlementManagementResourceRequest -BodyParameter $params`
explanation: Direct assignment is one of three ways an agent identity gets an access package (the agent requests it, a sponsor requests it, or an admin assigns it). In Graph PowerShell an admin assignment is an assignment request with requestType adminAdd that names the target, the policy and the access package.
rationale: Step 1: entitlement management cmdlets need the EntitlementManagement.ReadWrite.All scope, so you connect with it before any other call.
Step 2: the request needs the IDs of the access package and of its policy, so you read the package and expand assignmentPolicies.
Step 3: the body uses the values from step 2: adminAdd marks an administrator assignment, targetId is the agent identity, and the policy and package IDs come from $ap.
Step 4: New-MgEntitlementManagementAssignmentRequest submits the adminAdd request, and the agent identity receives the resource roles of the package.
Incorrect: this cmdlet creates a new assignment policy. The package already has a policy that allows All agents, so no new policy is needed. Use it when agents must be allowed to request a package.
Incorrect: Application.ReadWrite.All manages app registrations and service principals, not access package assignments, so the later cmdlets would fail. Use it to manage applications.
Incorrect: a resource request adds a resource such as a group to a catalog. The package already exists with its resources. Use it when you build a catalog before creating a package.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses and Microsoft Entra ID P2. An autonomous agent named Agent1 runs on a schedule and uses its own agent identity, created from an agent identity blueprint, to call Microsoft Graph. No user signs in to Agent1, and Agent1 has no agent's user account.

You need to block Agent1 from accessing all resources whenever Microsoft Entra ID Protection rates Agent1 as high risk.

Solution: You create a Conditional Access policy that is assigned to Agents and includes All agent identities, targets All resources, sets the Agent risk condition to High, and uses the Block grant control.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: For app-only agents the agent identity is the token subject, so the policy must be assigned to agent identities. The Agent risk condition uses ID Protection signals, and Block denies the token when the risk is high.
rationale: Correct: Agent1 requests tokens as its agent identity, so a policy assigned to agent identities with Agent risk set to High and a Block control denies access whenever ID Protection rates Agent1 high risk.
Incorrect: the solution does meet the goal. No would be right if the policy targeted users or agent users, because those subjects are not used by an app-only agent.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses and Microsoft Entra ID P2. An autonomous agent named Agent1 runs on a schedule and uses its own agent identity, created from an agent identity blueprint, to call Microsoft Graph. No user signs in to Agent1, and Agent1 has no agent's user account.

You need to block Agent1 from accessing all resources whenever Microsoft Entra ID Protection rates Agent1 as high risk.

Solution: You create a Conditional Access policy that is assigned to Users and includes the sponsors of Agent1, targets All resources, sets the Sign-in risk condition to High, and uses the Block grant control.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Policies assigned to users only cover agents that act on behalf of a signed-in user. An autonomous agent gets tokens as its own agent identity, so user policies and user sign-in risk never apply to it.
rationale: Incorrect: the sponsors are not the token subject. Agent1 signs in as its agent identity without a user, so this user policy is never evaluated for Agent1 and agent risk is not considered.

Correct: the solution does not meet the goal. A user policy with sign-in risk is right for agents that use the on-behalf-of flow; for Agent1 assign the policy to agent identities with the Agent risk condition.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses and Microsoft Entra ID P2. An autonomous agent named Agent1 runs on a schedule and uses its own agent identity, created from an agent identity blueprint, to call Microsoft Graph. No user signs in to Agent1, and Agent1 has no agent's user account.

You need to block Agent1 from accessing all resources whenever Microsoft Entra ID Protection rates Agent1 as high risk.

Solution: You create a Conditional Access policy that is assigned to Agents and includes All agent users, targets All resources, sets the Agent risk condition to High, and uses the Block grant control.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Agent identities and agents' user accounts are different token subjects. A policy that targets agent users does not apply to agent identities, and Agent1 has no agent's user account at all.
rationale: Incorrect: the policy covers agents' user accounts only. Agent1 authenticates with its agent identity, which this policy does not include, so a high-risk Agent1 still receives tokens.
Correct: the solution does not meet the goal. Targeting agent users is right for agents that act as digital workers with their own user account; Agent1 needs a policy that includes agent identities.

stem:
Lucerne Publishing uses an app that creates agent identities in Microsoft Entra Agent ID by using app-only requests. No user context is present when the app creates an agent identity.

You need to make sure that each create request succeeds.

Which relationship should the app set on each new agent identity?
choices: A sponsor
An owner
A manager
A service principal as owner
explanation: Sponsors are required when an agent identity or agent blueprint is created; owners and managers are optional. In delegated creation the calling user becomes sponsor automatically, but app-only creation must name at least one user or supported group as sponsor. Owners can be users or service principals, never groups.
rationale: Correct: a sponsor is mandatory at creation, and for app-only requests the creating service must set one or more users or supported groups as sponsor because no calling user can be added automatically.
Incorrect: owners are technical administrators of the agent and are optional for every agent identity object. Add owners when someone must manage credentials and configuration.
Incorrect: a manager places the agent in the organization hierarchy and can request access packages for the agent's user account. Managers are always optional.

Incorrect: a service principal can be an owner of an agent identity, which lets another service manage or delete it without user intervention, but owners are optional and do not satisfy the sponsor requirement. Use it when an automation service must administer the agents it creates.

stem:
Bellows College wants every member of the research IT team to have sponsor rights over an agent identity named Agent1. Membership of the team changes often and is managed by assigning users to a group manually.

Which group should you assign as the sponsor of Agent1?
choices: A Microsoft 365 group with assigned membership
A security group with assigned membership
A role-assignable security group
A role-assignable Microsoft 365 group
explanation: Agent identity sponsors can be users (including guests) or supported groups: dynamic membership groups (security or Microsoft 365) and assigned membership Microsoft 365 groups. Assigned security groups and role-assignable groups are not allowed. Every member of a sponsor group has sponsor rights.
rationale: Correct: an assigned membership Microsoft 365 group is a supported sponsor type, so every current member of the team gets sponsor rights and manual membership changes take effect.

Incorrect: assigned membership security groups are not allowed as sponsors of agent identities. A security group works only with dynamic membership. Use assigned security groups for resource access instead.
Incorrect: role-assignable groups are not supported as sponsors, whether security or Microsoft 365. Use them when the group must hold Microsoft Entra role assignments.
Incorrect: role-assignable Microsoft 365 groups are also excluded as sponsors. Use them only to assign directory roles to a group of people.

stem:
Margie's Travel has an agent identity named Agent1. User1 is a sponsor of Agent1 and has no admin role. During an incident, User1 disabled Agent1 from Manage agents in the My Account portal. The incident is now closed, and Agent1 must run again.

What should User1 do?
choices: Ask an owner of Agent1 to enable the agent
Select Enable agent for Agent1 in My Account
Request an access package for Agent1 in My Access
Add User1 as an owner of Agent1 in My Account
explanation: Sponsors hold business accountability with limited rights: they can disable, soft-delete and change sponsors, but they cannot re-enable or restore. Owners (or administrators) can re-enable, restore and hard-delete agent identities.
rationale: Correct: sponsors cannot re-enable an agent identity. An owner, or an administrator such as an Agent ID Administrator, must enable Agent1 again, which is the documented recovery path for sponsors.
Incorrect: Enable agent is available to owners, not sponsors. A sponsor who disabled an agent by mistake must contact an owner or admin. Use this option when you own the agent.

Incorrect: an access package grants resource access such as groups or roles. A disabled agent identity cannot obtain tokens regardless of its access. Use My Access when an enabled agent needs more access.
Incorrect: sponsors can modify the sponsors of an agent, not its owners. Owners, not sponsors, can add other owners. Ask an existing owner to add a new owner when needed.

stem:
Coho Winery deleted the account of an employee who left the company. The employee had built a shared agent with Microsoft Copilot Agent Builder, and the agent now appears under Agents without owners in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

User2 must get full edit and delete permissions for the agent.

Which action should you use?
choices: Assign new owner
Add owner
Pin for users
Update in store
explanation: For ownerless Agent Builder and Copilot Studio agents, administrators use Assign new owner. The new owner gets full edit and delete rights plus access to files that the previous owner uploaded. Add owner and Remove owner are for Agent Builder agents that still have an owner.
rationale: Correct: Assign new owner reassigns ownership of ownerless or active shared agents and gives the new owner full edit and delete permissions and the files of the previous owner.
Incorrect: Add owner adds another owner to an Agent Builder agent that already has an owner. For an ownerless agent, Learn directs you to the reassignment experience instead.
Incorrect: Pin for users makes a deployed agent more visible in Microsoft 365 Copilot. It changes visibility, not ownership. Use it to promote important agents.
Incorrect: Update in store replaces an existing agent in the Agent Store from a ZIP package. It does not change ownership. Use it to publish a new version of an agent.

stem:
Wide World Importers restructured several departments. More than 200 shared agents built with Microsoft Copilot Agent Builder lost their owners because their creators left. Each agent must be owned by the manager of its previous owner, as recorded in Microsoft Entra ID. Administrators must review the affected agents first, must complete the reassignment in a single bulk operation, and must not write scripts.

What should you do?
choices: Create and run an agent management rule that reassigns ownerless agents to manager
Create a leaver workflow that includes Transfer agent identity sponsorships to manager
Use Assign new owner on each agent that is listed under Agents without owners
Create and run an agent management rule that blocks ownerless agents without usage
explanation: Agent management rules in Agents > Settings run bulk governance actions after an admin reviews the impacted agents. The reassign rule supports only Agent Builder agents and moves ownership to the previous owner's manager based on the Entra hierarchy.
rationale: Correct: the Reassign ownerless agents rule identifies ownerless Agent Builder agents, lets you review them, and transfers ownership to the manager of the previous owner in bulk without scripting.

Incorrect: this Lifecycle Workflows task transfers sponsorship of Microsoft Entra agent identities, not ownership of Agent Builder agents in the registry, and it runs only for future leavers. Use it to keep agent identity sponsorship current.
Incorrect: Assign new owner works per agent and you would choose each new owner by hand, which does not scale to 200 agents. Use it for a single ownerless agent.
Incorrect: this rule blocks unused ownerless agents rather than assigning owners, so the agents would stop working. Use it to contain abandoned agents that nobody needs.

stem:
Graphic Design Institute uses Microsoft Entra Agent ID. You must give each person the narrowest administrative relationship on an agent identity named Agent1, without assigning any Microsoft Entra role.

Which relationship should you assign to each person? To answer, drag the appropriate relationships to the correct people. Each relationship may be used once, more than once, or not at all.
choices: Owner
Sponsor
Manager
Agent ID Administrator
explanation: Agent ID separates technical administration (owners), business accountability (sponsors) and organizational hierarchy (managers). These relationships are set per object and are separate from directory roles such as Agent ID Administrator.
rationale: User1 must restore Agent1 after a soft delete and manage its credentials, which only owners can do without a directory role.
User2 is accountable for the business purpose of Agent1 and must be able to disable it during an incident but must not change its configuration, which is the sponsor scope.
User3 must see Agent1's user account in the reporting line and request access packages for it, but must not modify or delete the agent, which matches the manager relationship.
targets: User1: restores Agent1 after a soft delete and manages its credentials
User2: accountable for Agent1's purpose and can disable it, but cannot change its settings
User3: sees Agent1's user account as a direct report and requests access packages for it
notes: Owner: technical administrator scoped to one agent object. Can edit settings, manage credentials, add owners and sponsors, re-enable, restore and hard-delete. Use it for developers or IT staff who run the agent.

Sponsor: business owner who is required at creation. Can disable, soft-delete and change sponsors, and requests access packages, but cannot change settings or re-enable. Use it for the accountable business person.
Manager: a user set in the hierarchy, usually on the agent's user account. Can request access packages for it and sees it as a report, but cannot modify or delete it. Use it for line accountability.

Agent ID Administrator: a Microsoft Entra directory role that manages all agent identities in the tenant. It is a role assignment, not a per-agent relationship, so the stem rules it out. Use it for central agent admins.

stem:
Trey Research has an agent identity named Agent1. User1 is the only sponsor of Agent1 and has no admin role and no ownership of Agent1. During a suspected incident, User1 must stop Agent1 from obtaining tokens, and must make sure that User2 shares business accountability for Agent1 from now on.

Which two actions should User1 perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Disable Agent1 from Manage agents in the My Account portal
Add User2 as a sponsor of Agent1
Add User2 as an owner of Agent1
Remove the credentials of Agent1
Hard-delete Agent1 and ask an owner to recreate it
explanation: Sponsors can disable agent identities, soft-delete them and change their sponsors. Technical operations, such as credentials, owners and hard deletion, belong to owners. Disabling blocks token issuance with the same effect as an admin disable.
rationale: Correct: sponsors can disable an agent identity from Manage agents in My Account, which blocks access and prevents token issuance, exactly as an admin disable would.
Correct: modifying the sponsors of an agent identity is within a sponsor's rights, and sponsorship is the relationship that carries business accountability.
Incorrect: sponsors cannot add owners; only owners and admins can. An owner is also a technical role, not business accountability. Use an owner for someone who manages configuration.
Incorrect: managing credentials is an owner capability, and User1 is not an owner. Rotate credentials as an owner after a confirmed compromise, before you re-enable the agent.
Incorrect: hard deletion is reserved for owners, and it destroys the identity instead of pausing it. Use permanent deletion only when the agent is retired for good.

stem:
Fourth Coffee has a shared agent named Agent1 that was built with Microsoft Copilot Agent Builder. User1 is the only owner of Agent1 and moves to another company next week. Until User1 leaves, both users must be able to edit Agent1. On User1's last day, User1 must stop being an owner.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence in the Microsoft 365 admin center? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: Go to Agents > All agents, filter Platform by Agent Builder, and select Agent1.
On the Details tab, select the user link next to Owner.
In the Owners pane, select Add owner, select User2, and then select Add.
Select User1, select Remove owner, and then select Remove.
Select Assign new owner, and then enter User2.
In the Owners pane, add the Sales security group as an owner.
explanation: Agent Builder agents support multiple owners with equal rights. You cannot remove the last remaining owner, so add the new owner before removing the old one. Assign new owner is the path for agents that are already ownerless.
rationale: Step 1: owner management starts from the agent details pane, and the Platform filter quickly narrows the registry to Agent Builder agents.
Step 2: the user link next to Owner on the Details tab opens the Owners pane, where owners are added and removed.
Step 3: User2 must be added first because the last remaining owner cannot be removed; after this step the agent has two owners with equal rights.
Step 4: with User2 in place, User1 is no longer the last owner and can be removed, which completes the handover.

Incorrect: Assign new owner replaces the owner, and the previous owner loses all access at once, so User1 could not keep editing until the last day. Use it for ownerless agents or an immediate handover.
Incorrect: groups are not supported as Agent Builder owners; an owner must be an individual user. Use a group as a sponsor of an Entra agent identity instead.

stem:
Adventure Works Cycles allows users to install agents built by Microsoft and agents built by its own developers. Users must not be able to install agents or plugins built by external developers.

Which setting should you configure in Agents > Settings in the Microsoft 365 admin center?
choices: Agent and plugin access
User access
Sharing
Agent feedback sharing
explanation: Agent settings in the Microsoft 365 admin center separate what kind of agents may be installed (Agent and plugin access, by publisher type), who may use agents (User access), who may share Agent Builder agents (Sharing), and whether developers get feedback.
rationale: Correct: Agent and plugin access has separate options for agents and plugins built by Microsoft, by your organization and by external publishers, so clearing the external publishers option meets the requirement.
Incorrect: User access chooses which users or groups can access agents and plugins at all. It does not distinguish publishers. Use it to limit agents to a pilot group.
Incorrect: Sharing controls who can share Agent Builder agents with others. It does not control installation of external agents. Use it to limit broad sharing.
Incorrect: Agent feedback sharing decides whether developers receive ratings and comments about agents. It has no effect on installation. Use it to help developers improve agents.

stem:
At Lamna Healthcare, users build agents with Microsoft Copilot Agent Builder. Only members of a group named ClinicalLeads may share their agents broadly with others in the organization.

How should you configure the Sharing setting in the Microsoft 365 admin center?
choices: Select Specific users, and then select ClinicalLeads
Select No users
Select All users
Set User access to ClinicalLeads
explanation: The Sharing setting has three options: All users, No users (no org-level sharing, but sharing with specific individuals still works) and Specific users (broad sharing only for selected groups). It only applies to Agent Builder agents.
rationale: Correct: Specific users restricts broad sharing permissions to designated groups, so only ClinicalLeads members can share their Agent Builder agents widely.
Incorrect: No users disables org-level sharing for everyone, including ClinicalLeads, while still allowing sharing with specific individuals. Use it when nobody may share broadly.
Incorrect: All users lets everyone share agents with others in the tenant, which violates the restriction. Use it when sharing is unrestricted.
Incorrect: User access controls who can access agents and plugins at all, not who can share. Setting it to ClinicalLeads would block every other user from using agents.

stem:
Humongous Insurance starts a pilot for agents in Microsoft 365. During the pilot, only members of a group named PilotUsers may access and install any agents or plugins. Other users keep their existing Microsoft 365 Copilot experience.

What should you configure in the Microsoft 365 admin center?
choices: Set User access to Specific users or groups, and select PilotUsers
Set Sharing to Specific users, and select PilotUsers
Clear every option in Agent and plugin access except for Microsoft
Set Available to on the Users tab of each agent to PilotUsers
explanation: User access is the tenant-wide gate for agents and plugins: All users (default), No users or Specific users or groups. Even users who are allowed to install an agent from the registry can use agents only if this setting includes them.
rationale: Correct: User access with Specific users or groups limits access to agents and plugins to PilotUsers for the whole tenant, while other users keep Copilot without agents.
Incorrect: Sharing only controls who can share Agent Builder agents broadly. Everyone could still install and use agents. Use it to limit sharing during a pilot.
Incorrect: this setting filters by publisher type for everyone, so all users could still install Microsoft agents and nobody gets a pilot boundary. Use it to block categories of agents.
Incorrect: Available to works per agent, so new agents would be open by default and you would have to maintain every agent. Use it to scope one specific agent.

stem:
Southridge Video sets the Sharing setting in Agents > Settings to No users. A week later, users still share agents that they built in Microsoft Copilot Studio with the entire organization.

What should you tell the security team?
choices: The Sharing setting applies only to agents built with Microsoft Copilot Agent Builder
The No users option still allows users to share agents with specific individuals
The Sharing setting takes effect only after you set User access to No users
The Sharing setting applies only to agents built by external publishers
explanation: The Sharing control in the Microsoft 365 admin center only governs agents built with Microsoft Copilot Agent Builder. Sharing of Copilot Studio agents is governed elsewhere, so a tenant can block Agent Builder sharing and still see Copilot Studio agents shared.
rationale: Correct: Learn states that the Sharing control only applies to agents built with Microsoft Copilot Agent Builder, so it has no effect on Copilot Studio agents shared with the organization.
Incorrect: this is true of No users, but it explains sharing with individuals only. The users in the stem share with the entire organization, which No users would stop for Agent Builder agents.
Incorrect: User access and Sharing are independent settings. No users in User access would block all agent use, which is a different outcome. Use it to turn off agents entirely.
Incorrect: external publisher agents are governed by Agent and plugin access, not Sharing. Sharing targets agents that users in your tenant build with Agent Builder.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses. User1 has the AI Administrator role. User1 must create a custom policy template named Template2 in Agents > Settings > Templates in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Template2 must assign an existing custom security attribute to the agents that are published with it. The attribute set and the attribute definition already exist. User1 must receive only the permissions that are required.

Which additional role should you assign to User1?
choices: Attribute Assignment Administrator
Attribute Definition Administrator
Conditional Access Administrator
Global Administrator
explanation: Custom policy templates add Entra policies (Conditional Access, access packages, custom security attributes) on top of the locked Microsoft default policies. The AI Administrator role alone is not enough for every custom policy: Learn states that both the Global Administrator and the AI Administrator need the Attribute Assignment Administrator role for custom security attribute policies, and that the AI Administrator lacks the privileges for Conditional Access.
rationale: Correct: Learn states that the AI Administrator needs the Attribute Assignment Administrator role to use custom security attribute policies in a template. The attribute already exists, so assigning it is the only missing permission.

Incorrect: Attribute Definition Administrator creates and manages attribute sets and attribute definitions, but it does not assign attribute values to objects. Use it when the custom security attribute must be defined first, which is already done here.

Incorrect: Conditional Access Administrator is the role to add when a template must include a Conditional Access policy for agents, because the AI Administrator cannot configure Conditional Access. Template2 contains no Conditional Access policy.

Incorrect: Global Administrator is far broader than needed, and Learn states that even a Global Administrator needs the Attribute Assignment Administrator role for custom security attribute policies. Use Global Administrator only for tasks that require it.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses. You have the Conditional Access Administrator and AI Administrator roles. A Conditional Access policy that blocks risky agents must be added to a custom policy template named Template1. The policy must apply only to agents that are published with Template1. Then a requested agent named Agent2 must be published with Template1.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: In the Microsoft Entra admin center, create a Conditional Access policy that applies to Agents and uses Select agents with at least one agent identity.
In the Microsoft 365 admin center, go to Agents > Settings > Templates > Add a New Template, and enter the name Template1.
Select Next, and then select the Conditional Access policy in the custom policies list.
Review the template, and then select Save template.
On the Requests tab, select Agent2, select Publish to store, and select Template1 in the template step.
In the Microsoft Entra admin center, create a Conditional Access policy that includes All agent identities.
Open the Microsoft default template, and add the Conditional Access policy to it.
explanation: Custom templates can only reference Entra policies that already exist, and a Conditional Access policy is listed only if it selects at least one agent identity. A policy scoped to all agent identities is selected automatically in the Microsoft 365 admin center and cannot be overridden. The template is then picked when an agent is published or activated.
rationale: Step 1: custom templates can only use policies created in Entra first, and only policies that select at least one agent identity appear when you build a template.
Step 2: with the policy in place, you start the template in Agents > Settings > Templates and give it its name.
Step 3: the custom policies list is where the Entra policy from step 1 is added to the template.
Step 4: saving the template makes it available in the template dropdown during publishing and activation.
Step 5: when you publish Agent2 from the Requests tab, the wizard lets you choose an existing, default or custom template, so you select Template1.

Incorrect: a policy scoped to all agent identities is selected automatically for every agent in the Microsoft 365 admin center and cannot be overridden, so it would not be limited to Template1 agents.
Incorrect: Microsoft built-in default policies are locked and cannot be edited, and the requirement is a custom template. Use the default template when its built-in controls are enough.

stem:
Coho Winery is configuring Agents > Settings in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

Which setting should you use for each requirement? To answer, drag the appropriate settings to the correct requirements. Each setting may be used once, more than once, or not at all.
choices: Agent and plugin access
Sharing
User access
Agent feedback sharing
Tags
Agent management rules
explanation: Each agent setting answers one question: which publishers (Agent and plugin access), who shares Agent Builder agents (Sharing), who uses agents (User access), whether developers get feedback, how agents are labeled (Tags), and which bulk actions run (Agent management rules).
rationale: Thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings and comments reaching the developers of selected agents is controlled by Agent feedback sharing with the Selected agents option.
A central list of labels with descriptions that admins and users apply to agents, up to 50 per organization, is managed on the Tags page.
Installing Microsoft first-party agents for all users in one reviewed bulk action is a supported scenario of agent management rules.
Blocking installation of agents and plugins from external developers is done by clearing the external publishers option in Agent and plugin access.
targets: Developers of the HR agent must receive user ratings and comments for that agent only
Admins must maintain the labels that people apply to organize and find agents
Install all eligible Microsoft-built agents for every user in one bulk action
Prevent users from installing agents built by external developers
notes: Agent and plugin access: allows agents and plugins by publisher type (Microsoft, your organization, external publishers). Use it to block whole categories of agents.
Sharing: All users, No users or Specific users for broad sharing of Agent Builder agents. Use it to control who may share agents they build.
User access: All users, No users or Specific users or groups who may access and install agents and plugins. Use it for pilots or to turn agents off.
Agent feedback sharing: No agents, All agents or Selected agents whose developers receive ratings and comments. It does not affect what agents can access.
Tags: admin-managed labels (up to 50) that admins and users apply to agents, each with an optional description. Use them to organize and filter the registry.
Agent management rules: reviewed bulk actions such as installing Microsoft agents, reassigning or blocking ownerless agents, applying a template, and rejecting old publish requests.

stem:
Refer to the case study. You need to configure Agents > Settings in the Microsoft 365 admin center to meet the business requirements for the pilot, for external agents, and for sharing.

How should you configure the settings? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
explanation: User access limits who may use agents at all, Agent and plugin access limits which publishers are allowed, and Sharing limits who may share Agent Builder agents broadly. Each requirement in the case maps to exactly one of these settings.

targets.label: User access
why: Incorrect: All users is the default and lets every employee, including seasonal staff, use agents, which breaks the pilot boundary.
Incorrect: No users blocks agents for everyone, including the pilot participants who must use them.
Correct: only pilot participants may use agents and plugins, and AgentPilot contains them, so Specific users or groups with AgentPilot meets the requirement.

targets.label: Sharing
why: Incorrect: All users lets everyone share Agent Builder agents broadly, but only guest services managers may.
Incorrect: No users stops broad sharing for everyone, including the guest services managers who must keep it.
Correct: Specific users restricts broad sharing to designated groups, so GuestServicesManagers are the only users who can share widely.

targets.label: Allow agents and plugins built by external publishers
why: Incorrect: leaving the option selected lets users install external agents such as Ski Rental Partner, which the requirements forbid.
Correct: clearing the option prevents users from installing agents and plugins from external publishers while Microsoft and organization agents stay allowed.

stem:
A. Datum Corporation uses agents built in Microsoft Copilot Studio, agents from external partners, and agents that do not have a Microsoft Entra agent identity.

You need a single inventory that includes all these agents.

Which location should you use?
choices: Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > All agents > Registry
Microsoft Entra admin center > Entra ID > Agents > Agent identities
Microsoft Entra admin center > Enterprise applications > All applications
Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > Tools > Registry
explanation: Agent registry experiences converge in Microsoft Agent 365: the registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center is the complete inventory, including agents without an Entra agent identity. The Entra admin center focuses on agent identities, blueprints and access controls.
rationale: Correct: the agent registry under Agents > All agents lists Microsoft agents, partner-built agents, agents published by your org and agents shared by creators, including agents without an Entra agent identity.
Incorrect: the Agent identities page shows only agents that have a Microsoft Entra agent identity. Use it to manage identities, blueprints and permissions.
Incorrect: Enterprise applications lists service principals and app registrations. It is not an agent inventory and misses agents without an Entra identity. Use it for app consent and SSO.
Incorrect: the Tools registry lists plugins, skills, MCP servers and connectors that agents use, not the agents. Use it to govern agent tools.

stem:
Blue Yonder Airlines wants an auditor to view the complete agent inventory in Agent 365 and the agents in Microsoft Entra Agent ID. The auditor must not be able to change any agent.

Which role should you assign by following the principle of least privilege?
choices: AI Reader
AI Administrator
Agent ID Administrator
Agent ID Developer
explanation: AI Reader is the recommended least-privilege role for viewing all agents in Agent 365 and Microsoft Entra Agent ID. AI Administrator manages agents in the Microsoft 365 admin center, and Agent ID Administrator manages agent identities.
rationale: Correct: Learn names AI Reader as the role for users who need visibility of all agents for monitoring or reporting, and it grants no change rights.
Incorrect: AI Administrator can view the inventory but can also publish, block and delete agents, which exceeds the read-only need. Use it for agent admins.
Incorrect: Agent ID Administrator is needed to manage or change agent identities, so it grants write access. Use it for identity admins of agents.
Incorrect: Agent ID Developer lets users create agent identity blueprints and does not give a tenant-wide read view. Use it for developers who build agents.

stem:
Wingtip Toys must review all agents in the agent registry whose makers uploaded files as knowledge sources.

Which filter should you use in the agent registry?
choices: Data source
Platform
Channel
Publisher type
explanation: Registry filters answer different questions: Publisher type (who owns and distributes the agent), Channel (where it is deployed), Platform (what it was built with), Status, and Data source (Embedded knowledge or Fine-tuned models).
rationale: Correct: the Data source filter has an Embedded knowledge option for agents that include files uploaded by the maker as knowledge sources.
Incorrect: Platform shows which product was used to create the agent, such as Copilot Studio or Agent Builder. Use it to find all agents from one build tool.
Incorrect: Channel shows where the agent is deployed, such as Copilot, Teams or Outlook. Use it to review agents on a specific surface.
Incorrect: Publisher type separates Microsoft, external partner, org-published and creator-shared agents. Use it to review agents by owner and distribution.

stem:
Consolidated Messenger deleted the accounts of 60 employees who left. Some of them had shared agents with colleagues. You need to quickly list the shared agents that no longer have a valid owner so that you can block or delete them.

What should you select in the agent registry?
choices: The Agents without owners card
The Unmanaged agents card
The Agents at risk tile
The Status filter set to Blocked
explanation: The registry summary cards are shortcuts: Agents without owners (shared agents whose creator was deleted), Unmanaged agents (agents outside Agent 365 protection) and Agents at risk (agents with risk signals). Each card filters the list with one click.
rationale: Correct: the Agents without owners card counts ownerless shared agents, updates when users are hard deleted, and filters the list so you can block or delete the agents.
Incorrect: Unmanaged agents counts agents created or managed outside Agent 365 without its risk protection and observability. Ownership plays no role. Use it to find agents to bring under management.
Incorrect: Agents at risk lists agents with risk signals from Entra, Defender or Purview. An ownerless agent might have no signals. Use it to prioritize security investigation.
Incorrect: the Blocked status shows agents that are already blocked, not the ownerless agents you still need to act on. Use it to review past block decisions.

stem:
In the agent registry of Munson's Pickles and Preserves, an agent built in Microsoft Copilot Studio appears twice: once as Shared by creator and once as Published by your org. An auditor reports the second row as an inventory error.

What should you tell the auditor?
choices: The rows are separate lifecycle and publisher records for one agent, and both are expected
The registry duplicated the agent, so deleting the Shared by creator row fixes the inventory
The agent was uploaded twice as a ZIP file, so one upload must be removed
The registry view is filtered by Channel, which shows one row for each channel
explanation: One Copilot Studio agent can have several registry entries with different publisher types. See agent in Microsoft 365 creates a Shared by creator entry, and admin publishing after approval creates a Published by your org entry. Removing one entry does not remove the other.
rationale: Correct: Learn states that duplicate-looking rows with different publisher types are by design; they represent separate lifecycle and publisher records of the same agent.
Incorrect: the rows are not a duplication error, and removing one entry does not remove the other, so deleting the creator entry changes the creator's testing view, not the published agent.
Incorrect: a ZIP upload through Add agent creates an org-managed entry, but nothing in the stem suggests an upload, and the publisher types show the Copilot Studio lifecycle.
Incorrect: Channel is a filter that narrows the list; it does not split one agent into rows per channel. Use it to focus on one deployment surface.

stem:
You review the agent registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center of Fabrikam, Inc. The summary shows Total agents, Agents without owners and Unmanaged agents. You apply the Publisher type filter and then export the list.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: After you apply the Publisher type filter, the Total agents count shows only the filtered agents.
Unmanaged agents counts agents that are created or managed outside Agent 365.
You can export only the filtered agents instead of all agents.
explanation: The registry summary reflects the whole tenant regardless of filters. Unmanaged agents identifies agents without Agent 365 risk protection and observability. Export to Excel can use the scope All agents or Filtered agents.
rationale: No: applying filters does not change the Total agents count, which always shows the number of agents in the tenant. Use the filtered list itself to see the subset.
Yes: Unmanaged agents is the number of agents created or managed outside Agent 365, without its risk protection and observability.
Yes: the export scope can be set to All agents or Filtered agents, so the export can match the Publisher type filter.

stem:
Trey Research has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses. You need a Microsoft Graph PowerShell script that reads the complete agent inventory, finds the agent named HR Helper, and retrieves its detailed metadata. The script must use the least privileged permission.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'CopilotPackages.Read.All'`
`$response = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/copilot/admin/catalog/packages"`
Call `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` with `$response.'@odata.nextLink'` until no next link is returned, and store the id of HR Helper in `$id`.
`Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/copilot/admin/catalog/packages/$id"`
`Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'CopilotPackages.ReadWrite.All'`
`Get-MgServicePrincipal -All`
explanation: The Package Management API exposes the registry: GET /copilot/admin/catalog/packages lists agents and GET /copilot/admin/catalog/packages/{id} returns details. Paging is server-driven, so follow @odata.nextLink until it is absent. CopilotPackages.Read.All is the least privileged permission for reading.
rationale: Step 1: CopilotPackages.Read.All is the least privileged permission for listing packages and getting details, so the session starts with it.
Step 2: the first GET on the packages collection returns the first page of agents in the tenant inventory.
Step 3: the collection is paged; requesting each @odata.nextLink until none is returned covers the whole inventory, and the id of HR Helper comes from these pages.
Step 4: with the id, the GET on packages/{id} returns the detailed metadata of HR Helper.
Incorrect: CopilotPackages.ReadWrite.All also works but is the higher privileged permission needed to block, unblock or update packages, so it violates least privilege.
Incorrect: this cmdlet lists service principals, which misses agents that have no Entra identity and returns no registry metadata. Use it to manage enterprise applications.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. has Microsoft 365 E5 and Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses. An administrator who has the AI Administrator role opens the agent registry and sees the full inventory, but the Risks column and the details on the Security tab of each agent are missing.

What should you do to make the risk information appear?
choices: Acquire Microsoft Agent 365 licenses for the tenant
Assign the Global Administrator role to the administrator
Assign the Security Reader role to the administrator
Acquire Microsoft Entra ID P2 licenses for the tenant
explanation: Viewing the agent inventory needs only a role such as AI Reader or AI Administrator. Risk signals in the registry, the Risks column and the Security tab need a Microsoft 365 E7 or Microsoft Agent 365 license, which Microsoft 365 E5 does not include.
rationale: Correct: Learn requires an E7 or Agent 365 license for the Risks column and the Security tab details, and the tenant has neither, so the license is the missing piece.
Incorrect: the problem is licensing, not permissions. AI Administrator already sees the inventory, and Global Administrator does not unlock features that the tenant is not licensed for.
Incorrect: Security Reader helps open the deep links to Entra and Defender for investigation, but it does not make the Risks column appear without the license.

Incorrect: Microsoft 365 E5 already includes Microsoft Entra ID P2, and no Entra license unlocks the registry risk signals, which require an E7 or Agent 365 license. Acquire Entra ID P2 when a tenant without it needs ID Protection features such as risk-based Conditional Access for users.

stem:
At Northwind Traders, developers build agents in Microsoft Copilot Studio and submit them for admin approval. You are an AI Administrator.

You need to find the submitted agents and review their capabilities, data sources and custom actions before they become available tenant-wide.

Which location should you use?
choices: Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > All agents > Requests
Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > All agents > Registry
Copilot Studio > Agents > Channels > Availability options
Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > Tools > Requests
explanation: When a member of the organization publishes an agent to the tenant, it waits on the Requests tab for admin approval. The admin reviews the agent metadata there and then publishes it to the store or rejects the submission.
rationale: Correct: the Requests tab lists agents that need admin review, with their full definition metadata, and offers Publish to store and Reject submission.
Incorrect: the Registry tab shows agents that are already available, installed or blocked. Submissions waiting for approval are on the Requests tab. Use the Registry for inventory tasks.
Incorrect: Availability options in Copilot Studio is where the maker downloads the ZIP or submits the agent. The admin review happens in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
Incorrect: the Requests tab under Tools holds requests for tools such as MCP servers and plugins, not agent submissions. Use it to approve MCP server registrations.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. has an agent named Agent1 that is published to the organization. A developer publishes an update to Agent1, and the request shows the state Pending update. Users must keep using the current version until you approve the change.

Which action should you select to approve the update after your review?
choices: Update in store
Publish to store
Approve request and activate
Add agent
explanation: The Requests tab shows three kinds of requests: pending review (new agents), pending update (new versions) and pending activate (template agents that users want to instantiate). Each has its own approval action, and users keep the previous version until an update is approved.
rationale: Correct: for a request in the Pending update state, you approve the new version with Update in store; until then users keep the previous version of Agent1.
Incorrect: Publish to store is the action for a new agent that is pending review. It starts the publishing wizard with users, template and permissions. Use it for first-time submissions.
Incorrect: Approve request and activate approves activation requests for template agents, so users can create instances. Use it for Agent 365 template agents.
Incorrect: Add agent uploads a ZIP package that you already have. The update was submitted by the developer and waits on the Requests tab, so no upload is needed.

stem:
A Microsoft-built agent is blocked in the tenant of Relecloud. User1 opens the agent in the store and selects Request. The request appears on the Requests tab with the state Allow user to install. User1 must be able to install the agent.

What should you do?
choices: Unblock the agent, and then approve the request of User1
Approve the request of User1, which unblocks the agent
Select Publish to store for the agent, and select User1
Select Approve request and activate for the agent
explanation: Users can request Microsoft-built agents that an admin policy makes unavailable. The request shows as Allow user to install. If the agent is blocked, it must be unblocked before a request can be accepted, and the org settings must also allow the user.
rationale: Correct: Learn says a blocked agent must be unblocked before any request to install it can be accepted, and then you approve the request so User1 can install the agent.
Incorrect: approving does not unblock the agent; a banner reminds you to unblock first. Approving alone leaves the agent unavailable to User1.
Incorrect: Publish to store applies to agents that your organization submitted for review. A Microsoft-built agent is already in the store and only needs the request approved.
Incorrect: Approve request and activate is for activation requests of template agents that users want to instantiate. Use it for Agent 365 template agents.

stem:
Wide World Importers has more than 300 agent publish requests. Many were submitted months ago by employees who no longer need them. You need to reject every publish request older than 60 days in one bulk operation that you review first.

What should you use?
choices: An agent management rule that rejects publish requests older than 60 days
An agent management rule that blocks ownerless agents without usage
Reject submission on each old request on the Requests tab
A Graph request that blocks each requested package
explanation: Agent management rules in Agents > Settings perform reviewed bulk actions. One supported scenario is rejecting agent publish requests older than a specified number of days, which clears a stale request queue without manual work.
rationale: Correct: the reject rule takes a number of days, shows the impacted requests for review and rejects them in bulk, which matches the requirement.
Incorrect: this rule blocks ownerless agents that have no usage. It does not process pending requests. Use it to contain abandoned shared agents.
Incorrect: Reject submission works, but one request at a time, which does not meet one bulk operation for more than 300 requests. Use it for individual reviews.
Incorrect: blocking a package prevents its usage but does not reject the pending publish request. Use the block endpoint to stop an agent that is already available.

stem:
At Litware, Inc., a developer submitted an agent named Agent4 for admin approval. Agent4 must become installable by the Sales group, must use the custom policy template Template1, and must have its requested Microsoft Graph permissions consented.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: Go to Agents > All agents > Requests, select Agent4, and review its capabilities, data sources and custom actions.
Select Publish to store, and select Sales as the users and groups who can install the agent.
Select Next, and apply the custom policy template Template1.
In Review permissions, review the requested permissions, and grant admin consent.
Select Next, and then select Publish.
Select Approve request and activate.
Select Update in store.
explanation: Publishing a requested agent follows the wizard: review the request, choose the audience, apply a template, consent to permissions and publish. The audience decides who can install, and an optional deploy step preinstalls the agent.
rationale: Step 1: the review starts on the Requests tab, where the agent details show capabilities, data sources, security and custom actions.
Step 2: Publish to store opens the wizard, and the first page selects the users or groups who can install the agent.
Step 3: after the audience, the wizard offers an existing, default or custom template, where you choose Template1.
Step 4: the Review permissions step shows the Graph permissions and is where admin consent is granted.
Step 5: after the review, Publish makes Agent4 available to the Sales group.
Incorrect: Approve request and activate handles activation of template agents so users can create instances. Agent4 is a new submission that needs publishing.
Incorrect: Update in store approves a new version of an agent that is already published. Agent4 is a first-time submission.

stem:
Tailspin Toys has Microsoft Agent 365 licenses. You need a read-only Microsoft Graph PowerShell script that lists the open requests from users who asked to publish an agent. The script must use the least privileged permission.

How should you complete the script? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes '[[1]]'
$uri = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/copilot/admin/catalog/packages?`$filter=[[2]] eq 'pending' and [[3]] eq 'publish'"
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri
```
explanation: The packages endpoint returns requested agents when you filter on request properties: requestStatus eq 'pending' selects the open queue and requestType selects publish, activate, access or update requests. Both can be joined with and.

why: Correct: CopilotPackages.Read.All is the least privileged permission for listing packages, and the script only reads.
Incorrect: CopilotPackages.ReadWrite.All is the higher privileged permission for block, unblock and update operations, which a read-only script does not need.
Incorrect: AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All manages the Teams app catalog, not the Agent 365 package catalog, and it grants write access.
Correct: requestStatus eq 'pending' is the supported expression that selects the open request queue.
Incorrect: requestType holds publish, activate, access or update, not pending, so the comparison would match nothing.
Incorrect: lastModifiedDateTime only supports ge and le bounds with a date value, not eq 'pending'.
Correct: requestType eq 'publish' narrows the queue to requests from users who asked to publish an agent.
Incorrect: requestStatus is already used for pending, and publish is not one of its supported filter values.
Incorrect: elementTypes describes package contents such as DeclarativeAgent, and request properties cannot be combined with it.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. has an agent named Agent3 that a developer submitted for admin approval. After approval, the Sales group must be able to install Agent3, the SalesManagers group must have Agent3 preinstalled, and the Microsoft default protections, including Microsoft Purview audit, must apply.

Which three actions should you perform in the publishing wizard? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Select Sales as the users and groups who can install the agent.
Select SalesManagers as the users and groups who will have the agent preinstalled.
Apply the default policy template.
Select Approve request and activate.
Pin the agent for SalesManagers in Manage pinned agents.
Select Update in store.
explanation: The publishing wizard separates availability (who can install) from deployment (who has the agent preinstalled), then applies a template and consents to permissions. The Microsoft default template includes Entra, SharePoint, Purview and Defender policies such as Purview audit.
rationale: Correct: the audience you select under publish is the set of users and groups who can install the agent, which is the Sales requirement.
Correct: the optional deploy step preinstalls the agent for the users or groups you select, so SalesManagers get Agent3 without action.
Correct: the default template brings Microsoft's essential security and compliance controls, including Purview audit, so no custom template is needed.
Incorrect: Approve request and activate handles activation of template agents, not publishing a submitted agent. Use it when users request to create agent instances.
Incorrect: pinning makes a deployed agent more visible but is not part of the publishing wizard and is not required here. Use it after deployment to promote an agent.
Incorrect: Update in store approves a new version of an agent that is already published. Agent3 is a new submission.

stem:
Refer to the case study. You review the agent requests for Lift Status, Trail Guide and Ski Rental Partner.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: Users continue to use the previous version of Lift Status until you approve the update.
Users can request Ski Rental Partner in the store, and you can approve that request on the Requests tab.
Selecting MountainOps as the users who can install Trail Guide when you publish it meets the Trail Guide requirement.
explanation: Pending update requests keep users on the previous version until approval. The user request and approval workflow in the Microsoft 365 admin center supports only Microsoft-built agents. Publishing to an audience makes an agent installable by that audience.
